title: Episode 25: Baby Doe Tabor: The Silver Queen and the Matchless Mine
description:
In the 1880s, Elizabeth 'Baby Doe' McCourt married Colorado's flamboyant 'Silver King' Horace Tabor, reigning over Denver society in peacock splendor. When the Silver Crash of 1893 destroyed their fortune, Horace on his deathbed whispered: 'Hold on to the Matchless, Baby, it will make millions again.' For the next thirty-six years, Baby Doe lived alone in a freezing wooden cabin beside the abandoned mine at 10,000 feet, wrapped in burlap rags, guarding the frozen shaft until the winter of 1935.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. The Gilded Age of the American West was filled with dazzling fortunes made and lost overnight, but no story is more tragic, romantic, or haunting than the rise and fall of Colorado's Silver Queen. In the eighteen eighties, Horace Tabor was the wealthiest mining baron in the Rocky Mountains, pouring millions into opera houses, mansions, and lavish jewels for his stunning young bride, Elizabeth 'Baby Doe' McCourt. But when the Silver Crash wiped out their empire, Horace died penniless, leaving Baby Doe with a single final plea: never sell the Matchless Mine. What followed was a thirty-six-year vigil of astonishing solitude and devotion two miles above sea level. Here is George with the story.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE SILVER KING OF LEADVILLE
In the late eighteen seventies, Horace Austin Warner Tabor was an unassuming, middle-aged stonecutter and shopkeeper in the high-altitude mining camp of Leadville, Colorado. His life changed forever in May eighteen seventy-eight when he grubstaked two destitute German prospectors, August Rische and George Hook, with sixty-four dollars worth of flour, bacon, and mining picks in exchange for a one-third interest in whatever they discovered. Just a few feet into the granite on Fryer Hill, the prospectors struck the Little Pittsburg vein—a solid wall of silver so fabulously rich that Tabor's sixty-dollar gamble yielded over a million dollars within months. Tabor used his windfall to buy up surrounding claims, most notably the Matchless Mine for one hundred and seventeen thousand dollars. The Matchless turned out to be a geological miracle, yielding pure horn silver that poured nearly ten thousand dollars a day into Tabor's pockets. Almost overnight, the quiet merchant was transformed into Colorado's undisputed 'Silver King.' Tabor spent his millions with reckless abandon: he built the grand Tabor Opera House in Leadville, constructed the palatial Tabor Grand Opera House in Denver with imported mahogany and Belgian crystal chandeliers, purchased private railroad cars, and was appointed to serve as a United States Senator in Washington.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: AUGUSTA AND THE SCANDAL OF THE DECADE
While Horace Tabor's wealth soared into the stratosphere, his marriage to his stern, puritanical wife Augusta deteriorated into open warfare. Augusta had spent two grueling decades running frontier boarding houses, baking bread, and washing laundry over open fires in remote mining gulches. She possessed a practical Yankee frugality, despised Horace's flamboyant spending, and warned him repeatedly that his wild extravagance and speculative investments would inevitably ruin them. Then, in eighteen eighty, Tabor met Elizabeth Bonduel McCourt. Known across the mining camps as 'Baby Doe' for her porcelain doll-like skin, golden blonde curls, and sparkling blue eyes, she was a spirited twenty-five-year-old who had arrived in Colorado from Wisconsin to work a gold claim with her first husband. When her marriage collapsed in abandonment, she caught the eye of the fifty-year-old silver baron. Tabor was utterly captivated by her youthful vivacity, warmth, and unshakeable admiration. Defying every strict Victorian convention of the era, Tabor secured a controversial, high-profile divorce from Augusta in a remote county court. Augusta fought the divorce bitterly in the Denver press, portraying herself as the loyal pioneer wife discarded for a young temptress. The scandal electrified Colorado society, drawing battle lines that would never heal.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE GILDED ZENITH IN WASHINGTON AND DENVER
In eighteen eighty-three, Horace Tabor and Baby Doe married in an event of staggering luxury at the Willard Hotel in Washington, D.C. At the time, Tabor was serving out an unexpired term as a United States Senator, and President Chester A. Arthur himself attended the wedding banquet alongside cabinet secretaries and foreign diplomats. Baby Doe wore a custom seventy-five-thousand-dollar wedding gown crafted from Parisian white satin and imported lace, adorned with the legendary Isabella jewels—a diamond necklace once owned by Queen Isabella of Spain, valued at over ninety thousand dollars. Yet beneath the glittering surface, social rejection was brutal. When the Catholic priest discovered both had been previously divorced, he refused to bless the union, and the wives of Washington's political elite boycotted the reception. Returning to Denver, Horace built Baby Doe an opulent Italianate mansion on Capitol Hill surrounded by bronze statues, velvet upholstery, and private peacocks roaming the gardens. But Denver's aristocratic society, fiercely loyal to the spurned Augusta, slammed every parlor door in Baby Doe's face. Undeterred, the couple lived in extravagant isolation, welcoming two daughters—Elizabeth, whom they nicknamed Lily, and Rosebud, affectionately known as Silver Dollar Tabor—surrounding their children with solid silver rattles, ponies, and private tutors.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE CATASTROPHIC SILVER CRASH OF 1893
The gilded dream shattered with apocalyptic speed in eighteen ninety-three. For over a decade, the United States government had artificially supported the silver market through the Sherman Silver Purchase Act, buying millions of ounces of silver each month to back paper currency. But when the Panic of eighteen ninety-three gripped Wall Street, President Grover Cleveland called a special session of Congress and repealed the Act to return the nation strictly to the gold standard. Overnight, the price of silver collapsed from over a dollar an ounce to less than sixty cents. Leadville's silver smelters blew out their fires, and hundreds of mines ceased operations. Tabor's fortune, built upon speculative real estate, unsecured bank loans, and the assumption that silver would remain valuable forever, evaporated in a matter of weeks. Creditors descended like vultures upon his assets. The Denver mansion, the private rail cars, the opera houses, and the mines were foreclosed and seized by federal marshals. Tabor was forced to sell Baby Doe's magnificent jewelry collection and family heirlooms for pennies on the dollar. Within three short years, Colorado's greatest multi-millionaire was completely destitute, reduced to renting a five-dollar-a-month room in a cheap boarding house.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE DYING COMMAND: HANG ON TO THE MATCHLESS
In his final years, Horace Tabor was humbled beyond imagination. At age sixty-seven, the former United States Senator and silver baron took a job with the Denver municipal public works department, swinging a pick and shovel in the gravel pits alongside day laborers for three dollars a day to put bread on his family's table. Through every humiliation, Baby Doe stood faithfully by his side, refusing to abandon him or return to her wealthy family in the East. In eighteen ninety-eight, sympathetic political allies persuaded President William McKinley to appoint Tabor as the postmaster of Denver, providing the family with modest financial dignity. But Horace's physical and mental health were irreparably shattered by the trauma of financial ruin. In April eighteen ninety-nine, Horace contracted acute appendicitis. Lying on his deathbed in the Windsor Hotel at age sixty-eight, Horace gripped Baby Doe's hand with his failing strength and uttered the fateful words that would seal her destiny: 'Hang on to the Matchless, Baby. It will make millions again when silver comes back. Never let it go.' Baby Doe wept and gave him her sacred promise: she would guard the Matchless Mine until the day she died.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE THIRTY-FIVE-YEAR FROZEN VIGIL AT FRYER HILL
True to her solemn vow, Baby Doe Tabor returned to Leadville in nineteen oh-two. She climbed the steep, wind-swept slopes of Fryer Hill to the long-abandoned Matchless Mine, taking up residence inside the mine hoist cabin—a crude, uninsulated twelve-by-sixteen-foot wooden shack perched ten thousand two hundred feet above sea level. For the next thirty-three years, the woman who had once dazzled Washington in Parisian silks lived as an impoverished hermit in the brutal climate of the Continental Divide. Winter temperatures regularly dropped to thirty-five degrees below zero, with snowdrifts burying the cabin up to the eaves. Baby Doe stuffed old newspapers into the cracks of the pine walls, hauled melting snow in tin buckets for drinking water, and burned scrap lumber and salvaged coal in a small cast-iron stove. Her daughters could not endure the squalor: Lily fled to Wisconsin to live with relatives, severing all contact, while Silver Dollar drifted into alcoholism and tragedy, dying mysteriously in a Chicago boarding house in nineteen twenty-five. Baby Doe was left utterly alone. She patched her dresses with rough burlap sacks, wrapped her feet in gunny sacks tied with twine, and wore an oversized miner's wool coat. Armed with an old double-barreled shotgun, she patrolled the abandoned mine shaft day and night, fiercely warning off scavengers and trespassers, convinced that the silver lode would soon roar back to life.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE CROSS IN THE SNOW AND THE ETERNAL LEGEND
The final chapter of Baby Doe's extraordinary vigil unfolded during the brutal winter of nineteen thirty-five. In early March, a howling blizzard paralyzed Leadville, dumping three feet of snow and dropping temperatures to forty below zero for nearly a week. When neighbors in town noticed that no smoke had curled from the cabin's crooked stovepipe for several days, a search party strapped on snowshoes and trudged through deep drifts up Fryer Hill. Pushing open the heavy wooden door, they found eighty-one-year-old Baby Doe lying on the bare pine floor, frozen solid in the arctic chill. Her arms were folded peacefully across her chest in the shape of a cross. On the rough wooden table beside her lay a stub of pencil, a kerosene lamp, and dozens of paper bags filled with diary entries recording her prayers, weather observations, and unyielding faith in Horace's return. The news flashed across wire services worldwide, capturing the romantic imagination of the nation. Today, the Matchless cabin is preserved as a state historical landmark, where visitors still stand in awe before the modest wooden shack and the dark, silent shaft. Baby Doe's tragic devotion was celebrated in Douglas Moore's celebrated American opera, The Ballad of Baby Doe, cementing her legacy as the Silver Queen whose love outlasted wealth, time, and the elements.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Baby Doe Tabor's life is an unforgettable testament to the romantic extremes of the American frontier—a tale where dazzling fortune gave way to a lifetime of unshakeable devotion against the brutal elements of the Rocky Mountains. Thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Join us next Tuesday as we travel to Utah for the driving of the Golden Spike. Until then, stay curious.
